h1: Developing house beers around your brewpub kitchen menu
title: House Beers Built Around Your Menu | Craft Beer School
desc: How to design a brewpub's house beers around its kitchen menu: auditing dishes, mapping flavours, choosing styles and testing pairings with real food.
teaser: Your chef and your brewer work twenty metres apart. Their menus should talk to each other.
standfirst: Most brewpubs write the food menu and the tap list separately, then hope they meet in the middle. Building house beers around what the kitchen actually cooks gives guests a reason to order both and gives staff something real to recommend.
sections: Why the beer list and the menu should meet

In a brewpub the food and the beer arrive at the same table. A guest eating a fiery Chettinad chicken with a 70 IBU double IPA will find the heat amplified and the beer harsh. Neither the chef nor the brewer did anything wrong. They simply never compared notes.

When house beers are designed with the menu in mind, servers can recommend with confidence, guests order a second round with the second course and the brewpub feels like one place rather than a restaurant with taps. Pairings also lift food sales, which matters because food often carries the margin in Indian brewpubs. Our guide to brewpub food menus and margins covers the kitchen side.

Sit down with the chef and list the dishes that sell most, not the ones the menu is proudest of. For each, note the dominant flavours and textures:

  • Heat from chilli and how intense it is.
  • Fat and richness, from butter, cream, ghee, coconut or cheese.
  • Acidity from tamarind, tomato, lime or vinegar.
  • Smoke and char from the tandoor or grill.
  • Sweetness, from caramelised onion, jaggery or sauces.
  • Spices that dominate, such as cardamom, clove, curry leaf or fennel.

A menu that leans on tandoori kebabs, butter chicken and biryani asks for different beers from one built on Goan seafood, Kerala fish curry and appam with stew.

Some general principles hold across most Indian food:

  • Carbonation and moderate bitterness cut through fat, which is why a crisp lager or Kölsch works with fried snacks and rich gravies.
  • High bitterness and high alcohol amplify chilli heat. Strong IPAs and fiery dishes rarely make friends. Our guide to beer and spicy food explains why.
  • Malt sweetness soothes heat and matches char, so amber lagers, Vienna lagers and brown ales work with tandoori food.
  • Wheat beers carry spice well. A witbier's coriander and orange peel sits naturally beside seafood and lightly spiced dishes, while a hefeweizen's clove and banana suits biryani.
  • Roast and body suit sweetness and richness, so a stout pairs with desserts and slow-cooked meat.

These are starting points, not rules. Your own beers and your chef's own recipes decide the final pairings. Our guide to Indian food and beer pairing has many more suggestions.

A small brewpub can usually keep four to six beers on tap. Rather than covering every style, cover the flavour ground the menu needs. A typical set might include a clean, crisp lager for heat and fried food, a wheat beer for spice and seafood, an amber or malty beer for tandoor and grill, a moderately hoppy pale ale for those who want hops without fire and a darker beer for dessert and richer meat dishes.

Then think about bitterness and strength. A house pale ale at a moderate bitterness and around 5 percent ABV will pair with far more of the menu than a 7 percent IPA at high bitterness. Keep the strong, bitter beers as specials for guests who want them.

Brew pilot batches or use existing beers, then run tastings with the chef, the brewer and the floor staff around the actual dishes. Taste each beer with each key dish and score whether the pairing lifts, clashes or does nothing. Make adjustments to the beer where needed: lower bitterness, a little more body, a slightly different hop. Sometimes the kitchen adjusts instead, with a squeeze of lime or a lighter hand on chilli.

Keep the tasting responsible: small pours, water and plain rice or bread on the table, spit cups available and non-drinking staff welcome to taste the food side. Record the results in a simple grid. It becomes your training sheet for servers.
Make it work on the floor

Pairings only matter if guests hear about them. Put one suggested beer beside key dishes on the menu. Train servers with a one-line reason for each pairing. Run a pairing evening once a month to show off a seasonal beer and a seasonal dish together. Track whether paired dishes and beers sell together. Keep the pairings that work.

In consulting work we often see brewpubs with excellent beer and excellent food that never meet on the plate. Closing that gap is usually a few weeks of tasting and a short menu change, not a new brewhouse.
faqs: Should every beer on tap pair with the food?
Most of the core range should pair with the dishes that sell most. Keep one or two beers for guests who want something strong or unusual, even if they pair with less.
What beer works best with spicy Indian food?
Crisp, well-carbonated beers with moderate bitterness and alcohol usually work best. Lagers, wheat beers and malty amber beers tend to calm heat, while strong, bitter IPAs amplify it.
Who should lead pairing development, the chef or the brewer?
Both, with floor staff in the room. The chef knows the dishes, the brewer knows what can change in the beer and the servers know what guests actually order.
